raw_text:
# Transcaval Access for Large-Bore Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

### Introduction
Large-bore arterial access is a cornerstone of modern structural heart disease therapies, most notably transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) [1]. Although the transfemoral approach remains the gold standard, calcific disease, severe tortuosity, or small vessel diameters in up to 10% of patients preclude safe transfemoral access [2, 3]. While alternative surgical routes like transapical, transaortic, and transaxillary routes have been developed, they carry significant surgical morbidity, requiring thoracotomy or general anesthesia and carrying risks of chest wall pain or pleural effusion [4, 5]. Transcaval access, first introduced in clinical practice by Greenbaum et al., has emerged as a completely percutaneous, highly feasible alternative that avoids the chest wall and pleural space entirely [1, 6].

### Anatomical Concepts and Pre-procedural Planning
The anatomical rationale of transcaval access rests on the proximity of the infrarenal abdominal aorta to the inferior vena cava (IVC) [7]. Pre-procedural planning relies heavily on multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) to identify a suitable, calcium-free window on the aortic wall directly adjacent to an accessible segment of the IVC, free from overlapping lumbar arteries or major retroperitoneal structures [6, 8]. This cross-sectional planning minimizes the risk of major retroperitoneal bleeding by ensuring that the retroperitoneal space is compressed by adjacent structures, allowing blood from the temporary shunt to decompress into the low-pressure venous system [9, 10].

### Procedural Technique
The procedure begins with femoral venous and contralateral femoral arterial access. A snare or target catheter is placed in the abdominal aorta from a superior or contralateral arterial access site, serving as a target [3, 11]. Under fluoroscopic guidance, a customized electrified wire system (typically an Astato wire or similar needle system connected to an electrosurgical generator) is advanced from the IVC, traversing the retroperitoneum to enter the abdominal aorta, where it is captured by the snare [12, 23]. Once cavo-aortic crossing is confirmed, the wire is exchanged for a stiff wire, and a large-bore sheath is advanced directly across the cavo-aortic tract into the aorta [13, 14]. After the structural intervention (e.g., TAVR or mechanical circulatory support [MCS] placement), the cavo-aortic tract is closed percutaneously, typically using an off-label nitinol cardiac occluder (such as the Amplatzer Ductal Occluder [ADO] I or II) delivered through the venous side [2, 11, 20].

### Clinical Evidence and Outcomes
The clinical utility of transcaval access was rigorously established in the prospective US Transcaval Registry, which demonstrated high procedural success rates (>98%) and low rates of major vascular complications in high-risk patients with no other viable transfemoral access options [2, 11]. Recent comparative analyses suggest that transcaval access is associated with shorter hospital lengths of stay and reduced intensive care unit utilization compared to surgical transthoracic approaches (transapical or transaortic) [10, 15]. When compared to other percutaneous options such as transaxillary or transcarotid access, transcaval access exhibits comparable rates of stroke and major bleeding, making it a robust alternative in the structural heart toolbelt [12, 19, 21]. Multi-center registries globally have corroborated these findings, reporting reproducible success rates and highlighting a rapid learning curve for experienced operators [13, 22, 25, 27, 28].

### Complications and Safety Profile
The primary safety concern of transcaval access is retroperitoneal hemorrhage [6, 24]. CT-based anatomical markers, including aortic calcification at the crossing site and high caval-aortic distance, are predictive of bleeding [24]. Furthermore, a persistent aortocaval fistula is expected immediately post-procedure; however, the majority of these shunts close spontaneously or remain hemodynamically silent during long-term follow-up [9, 26, 30]. Other rare complications include retroperitoneal hematoma, dissection, and aortic pseudoaneurysm [14, 16, 17].

### Expanded Indications and Future Horizons
Initially conceived for TAVR, the application of transcaval access has expanded to other large-bore procedures. These include thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR), endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), and the insertion of large-bore mechanical circulatory support devices like the Impella for cardiogenic shock or high-risk percutaneous coronary interventions [18, 29]. Dedicated closure devices engineered specifically for the cavo-aortic tract are currently undergoing clinical evaluation and promise to further simplify the procedure, reduce fluoroscopy times, and eliminate the off-label use of septal/ductal occluders [20].

### Conclusion
Transcaval access has revolutionized the management of patients requiring large-bore structural heart interventions who lack conventional arterial options. Through precise CT planning, standardized electrified crossing techniques, and reliable percutaneous closure, transcaval access provides a safe, fully percutaneous bridge that avoids the morbidity of surgical alternative routes.
